extracted.intended_audience: small law firms and SMMEs (small, medium and micro enterprises) operating in South Africa
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting, filing, prosecuting and maintaining trade mark rights in South Africa (CIPC processes, registrability requirements, examination and lifecycle). Aimed at practitioners and SMEs preparing trade mark applications and managing portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of territoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs are limited to the territory where they have been granted; an IPR registered in South Africa does not automatically give rights beyond the territory’s borders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the IPR is used in trade outside South Africa, protection must be sought in each territory where protection is required. International treaties facilitate cross-border protection but do not replace territorial filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of international filing routes (PCT, Madrid, Hague)
rubrics_metrics.description: States entered international treaties to enable protection abroad; the PCT provides a unified procedure for filing patent applications to protect inventions in contracting states; accession to the Madrid Protocol and Hague Agreement is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the PCT for unified patent filing across contracting states; consider Madrid Protocol for trade mark international registration and the Hague Agreement for designs once South Africa accedes. Treaties set minimum standards and can simplify multi-territory protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register with CIPC IPOnline and manage customer accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPC IPOnline is the official portal for IPR services in South Africa. You must register as a CIPC customer and create an IPOnline user profile to use the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users can create beneficiary accounts that will use funds from customer accounts for IP transactions. Register early, deposit funds as required, and use IPOnline for filing, searches and fee payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: CIPC institutional functions and interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPC manages registration/maintenance of trade marks, copyright, designs and patents; provides public disclosure via registers; monitors compliance; and promotes education and enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CIPC resources (website, practice notes, guidance) for filing formalities and to access legislation administered by CIPC. Familiarity with CIPC functions improves prosecution and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark types (ordinary, certification, collective)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three types of trade marks: ordinary marks (used by owner), certification marks (used by others under certification rules; owner may not trade in the certified goods/services), and collective marks (owned by an association and used by members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the correct mark type on application. For certification and collective marks, provide the rules governing use and, upon examination, provide a statement of case and affidavit evidence where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic representation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade mark must be capable of being represented graphically for users of the Trade Marks Office Register to identify the type of trade mark and the scope of protection granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure uploaded images or representations clearly show the mark and scope. Consult CIPC Guidelines on Examination (including annexures) for filing non-traditional marks and acceptable formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A trade mark is protectable only if it is distinctive — inherently capable of distinguishing the goods or services, or having acquired distinctiveness through prior use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive marks (indicating kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value or other characteristics) or marks that have become customary in trade are not registerable. The more distinctive a mark, the broader its protection. Consider adding distinctive elements or combining descriptive elements with distinctive features (descriptive elements may be disclaimed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited or non-registrable content (deceptive, generic, state emblems, immoral/offensive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks that are inherently deceptive, likely to confuse, contrary to law, contrary to morality, offensive to a group, or that contain protected state emblems/flags/official signs are not permitted for registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choosing marks that falsely suggest ingredients, cause consumer confusion, glorify illegal activities, contain offensive stereotypes/slurs, or use protected emblems. During examination, CIPC will request proof of consent if such elements are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing similarity to prior trade marks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is specifically prohibited to register a proposed trade mark that is identical or confusingly similar to a prior trade mark already registered by another proprietor or to a prior application in relation to the same or similar goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct a proper trade mark search before commencing use or filing. A refusal based on prior rights can sometimes be overcome by obtaining a written consent (coexistence agreement) from the owner of the prior mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark search recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a search of the Trade Marks Register to check the availability of the mark prior to commencing use or filing an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include a free cursory e-search, a paid commercial search on CIPC IPOnline, or requesting a special search from CIPC. Searches reduce risk of objection, opposition or refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for registration: single vs series; applicant eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When registering, you can apply for a single trade mark (one distinctive mark for specific products/services in one class) or a series of trade marks (variations of a core mark). Only the bona fide proprietor of the mark (used or intended to be used) may apply — a licensee cannot apply in their own name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose single or series appropriately. The applicant may be a natural person or juristic person; if filed in the name of a trust, cite the trustees correctly. Any change of name, transfer or assignment must be applied for at CIPC with prescribed forms and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant/contact details and address for service
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant’s address and any change of address must be recorded with CIPC. An address for service (physical address within South Africa) is required to receive correspondence from CIPC or third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applying without legal representation, ensure the address for service matches applicant details. Keep addresses up to date to avoid service/notification failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and Power of Attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: A Power of Attorney is required where the application is filed on behalf of the applicant. Only practising attorneys with valid Fidelity Fund Certificates may represent trade mark applicants; applicants may represent themselves; accountants and similar professionals may not represent applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure any representative is authorized and holds the required practising credentials. File Powers of Attorney as needed to avoid procedural delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of trade mark type on application (verbal vs image)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying, select ‘verbal’ for a word mark (typed in the form) or ‘image’ for a device trade mark (logo, stylised word, shape, configuration) and upload a representation of the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide high-quality image files for device marks and ensure the form fields correctly reflect the mark’s nature. For composite marks, be aware descriptive elements may be disclaimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of goods and services (Nice Classification) and class-based filing
rubrics_metrics.description: South Africa follows the Nice Classification for goods and services (45 classes). When filing, include the class number and ensure goods/services are properly described; separate applications are required for different classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm relevant classes and the correct class headings. Note updates (e.g., 12th Edition applies from 1 January 2025) and amend specifications accordingly to avoid scope issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade mark application process and lifecycle (TM1/TM3/TM5, examination, opposition, registration, renewal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications are filed manually using form TM1 or online via IPOnline after registering as a CIPC customer. The Registrar may accept, accept subject to amendments/conditions, or provisionally refuse. Upon acceptance the application is advertised in the Patent Journal, followed by a 3‑month opposition period. Registration is for 10 years and renewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for official actions and to respond to examination objections. Use prescribed forms (TM1 application, TM3 for advertisement? TM5 for registration certificate) and pay renewal fees on schedule to maintain rights. Track publication dates to manage opposition deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling descriptive elements and disclaimers in composite marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive words or elements can be included in an application as part of a composite or figurative mark, provided the composite meets distinctiveness requirements; descriptive elements will be disclaimed and the registration will not grant rights to the descriptive element separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining descriptive text with distinctive graphics, expect the descriptive part to be disclaimed. Design the composite so the overall mark remains distinctive and defensible.
